non-exam-assessment-independent-critical.d: Non-exam course: Independent Critical Study - Texts Across Time
terms: Feminism
Showalter Literature of Their Own 1977; Gilbert and Gubar Madwoman in Attic 1979; gynocriticism, female tradition.
Formalism and New Criticism
Brooks, Wimsatt 1930s-50s; intentional fallacy; close reading without biography; text as autonomous artefact.
Marxism
Lukacs, Eagleton; literature reflects class struggle; base-superstructure; ideology; Marxism and Literary Criticism 1976.
Psychoanalytic Criticism
Freud's Oedipus complex; Lacan's mirror stage and symbolic order; reads text as unconscious desire.
Reader-Response
Iser, Jauss 1970s; meaning produced in reading not text alone; horizon of expectations, implied reader.
Structuralism and Poststructuralism
Saussure's signifier/signified; Derrida's deconstruction 1967; meaning unstable; play of differences.

Atonement (Theme)
The novel asks whether art can ever make amends — and answers, with deliberate ambiguity, that it can only approximate.
Intertextuality
McEwan draws on Austen (epigraph from Northanger Abbey), Woolf, Forster, and Rosamond Lehmann; Briony writes within an inherited tradition.
Metafiction
Fiction that draws attention to its own status as constructed; Atonement's coda reveals the preceding narrative as Briony's novel.
The Coda
The 'London, 1999' section in which Briony reveals she invented Robbie and Cecilia's reunion; their real fates were death and grief.
Three-Part Structure
1935 (the country house), 1940 (Dunkirk and the hospital), 1999 (Briony's confession) — a temporal architecture mirroring atonement's stages.
Unreliable Narrator
A narrator whose account cannot be trusted; Briony's 1935 misreading and 1999 confession destabilise the entire text.

Fallen Woman Trope
A Victorian narrative figure marked by lost sexual 'purity' and consequent social ruin; Hardy interrogates and subverts it.
Fate vs Free Will
The novel's central tension: characters appear driven by cosmic chance and heredity rather than autonomous choice.
Paganism vs Christianity
Tess is linked to ancient sun-worship (Stonehenge climax) against the rigid, hypocritical Christianity of Angel and Alec.
Social Class and Heredity

Hardy's controversial 1891 subtitle that defends Tess's moral purity against Victorian convention, sparking outrage on publication.
Wessex
Hardy's semi-fictional reimagining of south-west England, a landscape that mirrors emotional and social states.

unit-4-internal-assessment-comparative-a.d: Unit 4: Internal course - Comparative and Contextual Study
terms: Biographical Criticism
Reads work through author's life; Plath's confessional poetry; criticised by New Criticism intentional fallacy.
Cultural Materialism
British Marxist; Dollimore and Sinfield Political Shakespeare 1985; contestation, dissident readings.
Eco-criticism
Lawrence Buell Environmental Imagination 1995; reads literature for ecological consciousness; nature writing tradition.
Historicism
Reads texts as products of historical conditions; e.g. Tillyard's Elizabethan World Picture 1943 for Shakespeare.
New Historicism
Greenblatt 1980s; texts and contexts mutually constitutive; Renaissance Self-Fashioning 1980.
Reception Theory
Jauss horizon of expectations; texts interpreted differently across periods; Hamlet's afterlife.
Comparative Reading
Setting two or more texts side by side to highlight similarities and differences in theme, technique and context.
Connective Vocabulary
Phrases like 'similarly', 'whereas', 'by contrast' that signal comparative moves to the reader.
Convergence and Divergence
Where texts agree, and where they diverge — both are fertile for argument.
Symmetrical vs Asymmetrical Comparison
Symmetrical treats both texts equally; asymmetrical uses one text to illuminate the other.
Tertium Comparationis
The third term — the framework against which two texts are compared.
Thematic Axis
A shared topic (power, gender, mortality) along which two texts can be aligned for comparison.
Base and Superstructure
Marx's model — economic base shapes the cultural superstructure (art, law, religion).
Defamiliarisation
Shklovsky's term — art renews perception by making the familiar strange (ostranenie).
Formalism
Critical approach (Russian Formalists, New Criticism) focused on the autonomous text — form, image, ambiguity.
Ideology
Althusser — the imaginary relation of subjects to their real conditions of existence, reproduced in texts.
Marxist Criticism
Approach reading literature as shaped by class, ideology and economic base (Eagleton, Williams).
New Criticism
Anglo-American formalism (Brooks, Wimsatt) advocating close reading and the intentional fallacy.

Bildungsroman
Coming-of-age narrative tracing moral and psychological growth; Goethe's Wilhelm Meister 1796 set the template; Joyce's Portrait of the Artist a modern instance.
Epistolary novel
Narrative told through letters or documents; Samuel Richardson's Pamela 1740 and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein 1818 use this form.
Free indirect discourse
Third-person narration coloured by a character's voice without quotation marks; pioneered by Jane Austen in Emma 1815.
Magic realism
Fusion of realistic settings with matter-of-fact magical elements; Gabriel Garcia Marquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude 1967 is the canonical example.
Novel of manners
Genre satirising social customs of a defined class; Austen's Pride and Prejudice 1813 and Edith Wharton's Age of Innocence 1920 are paradigms.
Unreliable narrator
Wayne Booth's 1961 term for narrators whose account the reader must distrust; Nabokov's Humbert Humbert in Lolita 1955 typifies it.

Wordsworth Prelude
Autobiographical epic in blank verse; spots of time; growth of poet's mind; 1805 and 1850 versions.
Epistolary Form
A novel composed of letters, diary entries, news cuttings, and phonograph transcripts; Stoker's form mimics evidentiary accumulation.
Fin de Siècle
The 'end of the century' (1890s) atmosphere of decadence, decline, and anxiety over degeneration.
Lucy and Mina
Stoker's dual heroines: Lucy is sexualised, infected and destroyed; Mina is intellectual, infected and saved — a Madonna/whore split.
New Woman
1890s figure of female emancipation; Mina exhibits 'New Woman' competence (stenography, intellect) while remaining domestically anchored.
Reverse Colonisation
Stephen Arata's term (1990) for the anxiety that the colonial periphery (Transylvania) might invade and contaminate the imperial centre (London).
Van Helsing's Polyglossia
Van Helsing's mangled English, scientific authority, and folkloric knowledge model Stoker's hybrid epistemology — modern + ancient.
Frame Narrative
Walton's letters frame Victor's narrative, which frames the Creature's; nested narration foregrounds testimony and reliability.
Galvanism
Luigi Galvani's late-18th-century experiments with electricity and frog legs; haunts Shelley's vivification scene without being named.
Gothic Conventions
Atmospheric setting, doubling, transgression, the uncanny, supernatural intrusion — Shelley fuses Gothic with Enlightenment science.
Promethean Myth
Greek myth of the Titan who steals fire from the gods; Shelley's subtitle 'The Modern Prometheus' frames Victor as transgressor.
Romanticism
Late-18th/early-19th-century movement valuing imagination, nature, and individual subjectivity; Shelley engages and critiques it.
Sublime
Burkean and Kantian category of overwhelming, terrifying grandeur; the Alps and Arctic embody it, mirroring Victor's ambition.
Antic Disposition
Hamlet's feigned madness, declared at 1.5; its boundaries with real disturbance remain critically contested.
Hamartia
Aristotelian 'tragic flaw'; for Hamlet, variously identified as melancholy, indecision, intellectualism, or moral scruple.
Quarto and Folio Texts
Q1 (1603, 'bad quarto'), Q2 (1604/5, longest), F1 (1623); textual variants make 'Hamlet' a plural work.
Revenge Tragedy
Genre popularised by Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy (1587); features ghost, delay, madness real or feigned, play-within-a-play, bloody finale.
Soliloquy
A speech delivered alone on stage, granting audience access to a character's interiority; Hamlet has seven major soliloquies.
The Ghost
Old Hamlet's spectre, theologically ambiguous (purgatorial Catholic? demonic Protestant?) — a hermeneutic crisis as much as a plot device.
Affective Fallacy
Wimsatt & Beardsley — appealing to reader emotion is also fallacious.
Binary Opposition
Lévi-Strauss — culture organises meaning through binary pairs (raw/cooked, nature/culture).
Intentional Fallacy
Wimsatt & Beardsley (1946) — appealing to authorial intention is fallacious; the text is sovereign.
New Criticism
Anglo-American formalist school (Brooks, Ransom, Wimsatt) advocating close reading of the autonomous text.
Signifier and Signified
Saussure's two halves of the sign — the sound-image and the concept; relation is arbitrary.
Structuralism
Movement (Saussure, Lévi-Strauss, Barthes early) treating culture as a system of signs.
Eliot Waste Land 1922
Fragmented epic of post-WWI Europe; allusions to Dante, Buddhist sermons; 'shored against my ruins'.
HD (Hilda Doolittle)
Imagist; classical refigured ('Helen', 'Sea Garden'); sharp imagery, free verse.
Pound Make It New
Imagism 1934 (the book title); In a Station of the Metro; 'direct treatment of the thing'; clarity, concision.
Stein Tender Buttons 1914
Gertrude Stein's Cubist prose poetry; cuts ordinary language to renew perception.
Williams Red Wheelbarrow
1923; 'so much depends'; American Imagism; everyday objects with attention; against Eliot's tradition.
Yeats Tower Period
Second Coming 1919-20; 'things fall apart; the centre cannot hold'; mysticism and Irish history.
Focalisation
Whose perspective filters narrative information — zero, internal or external.
Frequency
How often events are told relative to occurrence — singulative, repetitive, iterative.
Genette's Narrative Discourse (1972)
Foundational narratological study analysing Proust through systematic categories.
Narrative Duration
How story-time maps to discourse-time — scene, summary, ellipsis, pause.
Narrative Order
The relation between story-time and discourse-time — analepsis (flashback), prolepsis (flash-forward).
Narrative Voice
Who speaks — heterodiegetic (outside) or homodiegetic (inside) the story.

non-exam-assessment-literature-post-1900.d: Non-exam course: Literature post-1900 (Close Reading and Comparative Essay)
terms: Angry Young Men
1950s movement: Osborne's Look Back in Anger 1956, Amis Lucky Jim 1954; class resentment, anti-establishment.
Black British Poetry
Linton Kwesi Johnson, Grace Nichols; Patience Agbabi; reframes English tradition with Caribbean and African voices.
Carter Bloody Chamber 1979
Angela Carter's feminist fairy tale rewrites; subverts Bluebeard, Beauty and Beast; magical realism.
Heaney North 1975
Bog poems use Iron Age bodies to address Northern Ireland Troubles; Catholic Irish poet; Nobel 1995.
Larkin The Less Deceived 1955
The Movement; plain diction, anti-modernist; ironic Englishness; 'Church Going', 'Whitsun Weddings'.
Plath Ariel 1965
Confessional poetry; 'Daddy', 'Lady Lazarus'; published posthumously after 1963 suicide; Bell Jar same year.

Calvinist Theology
Doctrine of predestination — the elect and reprobate are eternally determined; complicates whether Faustus could ever have been saved.
Mephistopheles
Faustus's attendant devil; theologically lucid, often warns Faustus, and embodies the tragedy of self-aware damnation.
Morality Play
Medieval allegorical drama (e.g. Everyman, c.1500) in which abstract virtues and vices contend for the soul; Marlowe's Good and Bad Angels are direct inheritances.
Necromancy
The conjuring of spirits; Faustus's chosen art, theologically distinct from natural magic and condemned by both Protestant and Catholic authorities.
Renaissance Humanism
Recovery of classical learning, emphasis on human capacity and intellectual ambition; Faustus exemplifies its dangerous extremity.
The Seven Deadly Sins Pageant
In 2.3 Lucifer parades Pride, Covetousness, Wrath, Envy, Gluttony, Sloth, Lechery before Faustus — a direct morality-play borrowing.
Cinthio's Hecatommithi
Giraldi Cinthio's 1565 Italian novella collection; the seventh story of the third decade provides Shakespeare's plot — 'Disdemona' and an unnamed 'Moor'.
Domestic Tragedy
The play borrows from the emerging genre of bourgeois domestic tragedy (Arden of Faversham, A Woman Killed with Kindness) by locating tragedy in marriage.
Iago
The play's longest part (more lines than Othello); a Vice-figure descendant who weaponises his audience access through soliloquy.
Jealousy as Theme
Iago calls it 'the green-eyed monster'; the play anatomises jealousy as epistemic rather than purely emotional — a way of misreading the world.
Race and Moorishness
Othello is repeatedly called 'Moor', 'thick-lips', 'the Barbary horse' — Shakespeare stages early modern racial categories with critical sharpness.
Tragic Hero
Aristotelian protagonist of stature whose hamartia precipitates downfall; Othello's stature is racially marked, his fall amplified.
Lockwood arrives in 1801, returns in 1802; the action stretches back to 1771 (Heathcliff's arrival as a child).
Diary and Document
Catherine's marginalia in Lockwood's borrowed books opens the past; the novel embeds textual layers within the oral frame.
Frame Narrative
Lockwood, the southern outsider tenant of Thrushcross Grange, frames Nelly Dean's interior narration of the Earnshaw-Linton history.
Lockwood
Naive, snobbish, and unreliable; his misreadings (of Catherine's diary, of Heathcliff's character) prime the reader to be sceptical.
Nelly Dean
Housekeeper and lifelong witness; her narration is intimate but partisan — she dislikes Heathcliff and favours the Lintons.
Publication
Published in three volumes in December 1847 under 'Ellis Bell'; Charlotte's 1850 preface introduced Emily's name and softened reception.

Culture and Imperialism (1993)
Said's sequel reading canonical novels (Mansfield Park, Heart of Darkness) for their imperial assumptions.
Foucauldian Frame
Said borrows Foucault's idea that knowledge and power are inseparable — discourse produces what it claims to describe.
Imaginative Geography
Said's term for the symbolic mapping of self and other onto territory.
Latent and Manifest Orientalism
Said distinguishes the persistent unconscious orientalist substrate from its surface manifestations.
Orientalism (1978)
Edward Said's foundational study — Western academic and aesthetic representations of 'the East' produced and supported colonial power.
Othering
The discursive construction of a group as different and inferior — a key post-colonial mechanism.
First-Person Narration
The narrator is a character within the story (I went.), offering immediacy and bias.
Multiple Narrators
Texts using several first-person voices (The Sound and the Fury, As I Lay Dying).
Second-Person Narration
Rare 'you' narration (Bright Lights, Big City) that implicates the reader.
Third-Person Limited
Narrator stands outside but restricts knowledge to one character's perspective.
Third-Person Omniscient
Narrator stands outside the story with access to all characters' thoughts and events.
Unreliable Narrator
Wayne Booth (1961) — narrator whose account the reader is invited to distrust.
